question: If the temperature of a gas is increased at constant volume, what happens to the pressure?
solution:
The correct answer is __**It increases**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• According to **Gay-Lussac’s Law**, the **pressure** of a given mass of gas is **directly proportional** to its absolute **temperature**, provided the **volume** remains **constant**.
 
• When the **temperature** of a gas increases, the **average kinetic energy** of the gas molecules also increases. This causes the molecules to move at **higher velocities**.
 
• As the molecules move faster, they collide with the walls of the container more **frequently** and with **greater force**. Since **pressure** is defined as the force exerted per unit area, these intensified collisions result in an **increase in pressure**.
 
• This relationship can be mathematically expressed as **P/T = k** (where k is a constant) or **P1/T1 = P2/T2**. This implies that if the **temperature** (T) increases, the **pressure** (P) must also increase to maintain the constant ratio. ***Hence, the statement that pressure increases is correct.***
 
• The **temperature** in these gas law calculations must always be exp
